questions.q: In a station or platform emergency, who commands the incident locally at the start?
options: The first passenger to raise the alarm
The station controller, until Operations Control Centre (OCC) or an external agency takes over
The train operator at the platform
The station's senior-most shopkeeper
questions.explain: Local command starts with the station controller — Operations Control Centre (OCC)/agency command replaces it as the response builds.

questions.q: During a platform emergency, trains must be protected by:
options: Stopping them, or skipping them past the affected platform/station
Speeding them through the platform
Letting them stop as scheduled regardless
Reversing them to the depot
questions.explain: A train arriving into an emergency adds crowd and danger — it is held away or run through as directed.

questions.q: After an earthquake, trains may resume only after:
options: One hour has passed
Passengers demand resumption
Structures and track are inspected, with a speed-restricted inspection run first
The tremors are no longer felt in the office
questions.explain: Earthquakes damage silently — inspection and a restricted trial run come before passengers at speed.

questions.q: Why is the first run after an earthquake kept at restricted speed?
options: Because passengers are frightened of speed
To save fuel after the incident
Because the timetable has been cancelled
To inspect the track and structures from the train and stop safely if damage is found
questions.explain: The inspection run is a moving examination — its speed is set by stopping distance, not the timetable.

questions.q: In flooding or waterlogging, trains must stop where:
options: Water threatens the track or electrical equipment
The platform is slightly wet
Rain is falling anywhere in the city
A drain outside the station overflows
questions.explain: Water and electrical equipment are a dangerous mix — the threat to track/electrics is the stopping line.

questions.q: A suspicious unattended object is found on a platform. Staff must:
options: Pick it up and take it to the lost-property office
Not touch it, cordon the area, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) and follow police direction
Open it to check whether it is dangerous
Ask passengers to gather around and identify it
questions.explain: Untouched and cordoned is safe; handling a suspect object is how staff become casualties.

questions.q: During a security threat at a station, the controlling authority for the security response is:
options: The station controller alone
Operations Control Centre (OCC) alone, overruling the police
The police, with railway staff supporting and following their direction
The passengers' majority view
questions.explain: Security is a police subject — the railway protects trains and people and follows police direction.

questions.q: In extreme heat or a storm, the typical operational precautions include:
options: Temporary speed restrictions, and vigilance for Overhead Equipment (OHE) problems and fallen trees
Increasing speeds to finish services early
Cancelling all maintenance for the season
Opening tunnel doors for ventilation
questions.explain: Heat and storm attack the overhead equipment and the trackside — Temporary Speed Restrictions (TSRs) and vigilance are the standard response.

questions.q: A fire breaks out in a shop inside the station concourse. The station response should:
options: Only inform the shopkeeper's company
Close only the shop and continue everything else silently
Use the platform as the assembly point regardless
Raise the alarm, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), isolate/evacuate the affected area and guide passengers away, calling fire services
questions.explain: A concourse fire is a station emergency — alarm, control, evacuation of the area and the fire brigade.

questions.q: A passenger is injured by a falling object on a platform. Along with first aid, staff must:
options: Move the object and clean the platform at once
Protect the area, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC)/station control and arrange medical help, preserving facts for the report
Ask the passenger to go home and rest
Announce his name to trace his family first
questions.explain: Care for the person, protect others from the same hazard, and keep the facts for the incident record.

questions.q: A crowd surges dangerously as a popular train arrives. The station controller's immediate tools are:
options: Stop further entry, use announcements, open additional exits/flows and regulate the platform crowd
Close all exits to hold people in place
Let the crowd settle by itself
Cancel the train after it has arrived
questions.explain: Crowd control works on inflow and outflow — stop entry, widen exit, inform.

questions.q: A Platform Screen Door (PSD) fails to open with a train standing at the platform. Staff should:
options: Force all doors open with crowbars
Ask passengers to climb through the driver's cab
Follow the prescribed Platform Screen Door (PSD) failure procedure and Operations Control Centre (OCC) instructions, detraining passengers by the authorised method
Cancel the railway for the day
questions.explain: Platform Screen Door (PSD) failures have a laid-down procedure — improvised forcing damages equipment and endangers passengers.

questions.q: An external emergency in the city (major accident nearby) floods the station with casualties' relatives and crowds. The station should:
options: Close the station without informing anyone
Inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), manage the crowd, support agency direction and keep train operations protected
Stop all trains in the network
Turn the platform into a treatment ward
questions.explain: The station supports the city's response without losing control of its own crowds and trains.

questions.q: A tree falls across the track ahead during a storm. The first operational action is to:
options: Send the next train slowly to push it aside
Ask passengers to help clear it
Wait for the morning inspection only
Stop or protect trains approaching that section and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: An obstruction is protected first — trains are stopped before anyone plans the clearance.

questions.q: Water begins entering a station from flooded streets. Priorities include:
options: Protecting people and electrical installations, stopping entry of water where possible and informing Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Keeping ticket sales running at all costs
Moving all passengers to the lowest floor
Switching on all electrical equipment to test it
questions.explain: Flood response protects life and electrics first — water and power together are the danger.

questions.q: After a storm passes, normal speeds resume when:
options: The rain stops
The wind drops for ten minutes
The line has been inspected and certified fit, including Overhead Equipment (OHE) and trackside
Passengers stop reporting problems
questions.explain: Resumption follows inspection and certification, not the weather clearing alone.

questions.q: A bomb-threat call is received for a specific train. The response runs on:
options: Police/security direction, with the train and area handled exactly as the security plan prescribes
The train operator's personal judgement
Immediate detrainment wherever the train stands, always
Announcements asking passengers to search the train
questions.explain: Threat calls are security operations — searching and movement follow the police-led plan.

questions.q: During a platform emergency, announcements should avoid:
options: Giving the evacuation route
Creating panic with alarming, unclear or contradictory messages
Telling passengers what not to do
Repeating the message at intervals
questions.explain: Calm, clear and consistent information moves crowds; alarm and contradiction freeze or stampede them.

questions.q: A structural problem (cracked beam) is noticed in a station building. The immediate steps are:
options: Paint over the crack and monitor it
Let passengers use the area as the crack is small
Announce that the station is closing forever
Cordon the area below/around it, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) and arrange engineering inspection, restricting access until certified
questions.explain: A cordon plus engineering certification — nobody waits under a suspect structure.

questions.q: An escalator fails suddenly with passengers on it during peak hours. Staff should:
options: Restart it repeatedly until it works
Blame the passengers standing on it
Stop/secure it as per procedure, assist any injured, inform control and manage the crowd flow around it
Close the whole station for the day
questions.explain: Secure the machine, care for people, and re-route the crowd — the standard local emergency pattern.

questions.q: Why are trains sometimes ordered to skip a station during that station's emergency?
options: To punish the station staff
To avoid adding passengers and crowd to a station that is being evacuated or controlled
Because the train is running late anyway
To save electricity at that station
questions.explain: A stopping train feeds the problem; skipping protects both the train and the station crowd.

questions.q: A major external power-grid failure blacks out a whole area including stations. Station priorities are:
options: Backup power for essential services, passenger safety and information, and regulated train service as systems allow
Immediate evacuation of every station in all cases
Running trains at full speed in darkness
Closing the network without information
questions.explain: Essential services on backup, people informed and safe, service matched to what the systems can support.

questions.q: Passengers must be kept off a platform where an emergency is in progress mainly because:
options: The platform is being cleaned
Tickets cannot be checked there
An uncontrolled crowd at the incident site endangers both themselves and the responders' work
The trains are all cancelled permanently
questions.explain: The incident site is a workplace for responders — crowds there become second incidents.

questions.q: After an external emergency ends, the lessons and facts are captured through:
options: Word of mouth among staff
The next day's newspaper
Passengers' social media posts
The incident report and debrief, feeding lessons learned into procedures
questions.explain: Reporting and debrief turn one emergency into protection against the next.

questions.q: A passenger reports a strong gas smell in a station. Staff should:
options: Light a match to locate the leak
Raise the alarm, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), avoid sparks/electrical switching in the area, evacuate as directed and call the appropriate agencies
Ignore it as a drain smell
Open all electrical panels to ventilate
questions.explain: A gas smell is treated as real until proven otherwise — no ignition sources, evacuate, escalate.

questions.q: During a heat wave, a passenger faints on a platform. This is handled as:
options: A medical emergency — first aid, shade/cool place, inform control and arrange medical help if needed
A security incident
A reason to stop all trains
A passenger's personal problem, not staff's concern
questions.explain: A faint is a medical case — the same first aid, information and handover chain applies.

questions.q: The station controller hands over local command when Operations Control Centre (OCC)/agency takes over. A good handover includes:
options: Only the time the incident started
The list of trains delayed
Situation, actions already taken, casualties, hazards and what help is on site or coming
His personal opinion of the cause
questions.explain: Continuity of command depends on a complete brief — the new commander starts from facts, not zero.

questions.q: A platform is overcrowded because trains are delayed, though no incident has occurred. The controller should still:
options: Wait until an incident occurs before acting
Apply crowd management early — stop or meter entry and keep announcements flowing
Open the platform edge doors to the track
Ask passengers to stand closer together
questions.explain: Crowd risk is managed before it becomes an emergency — early metering prevents the crush.

questions.q: Which external emergency and first response pairing is correct?
options: Earthquake — stop trains and inspect before resuming
Earthquake — resume at full speed after 10 minutes
Flood — run trains faster through water
Security threat — staff open and search suspicious bags
questions.explain: Each external threat has a signature first move; for earthquakes it is stop and inspect.

questions.q: A fire alarm activates in an unstaffed station area at night. The response is driven by:
options: Nobody, until morning staff arrive
Passengers who happen to be present
The cleaning contractor alone
Operations Control Centre (OCC)/station control acting on the alarm information, dispatching staff/agencies as the plan prescribes
questions.explain: Alarms are monitored centrally — an unstaffed location still gets a planned response.

questions.q: A platform is filling faster than trains can clear it, though no incident has happened yet. The most effective preventive action at the station's control point is:
options: Making louder announcements
Temporarily stopping or metering passenger entry at the gates so the platform crowd stays within safe limits
Asking passengers to stand closer together
Opening more ticket windows
questions.explain: Crowd disasters are prevented at the entry, not on the platform. Holding people at concourse or gate level — where there is space — keeps platform density survivable.

questions.q: A thunderstorm with lightning is directly over an open section where staff are working on the Overhead Equipment (OHE). The correct safety action is:
options: Finish the work quickly before rain starts
Suspend the work, bring staff down and clear of the equipment and track area until the storm passes
Continue working but avoid touching metal
Work only on one wire at a time
questions.explain: Lightning can strike the Overhead Equipment (OHE) and structures without warning. No maintenance task is worth a life — work stops and staff take shelter till the storm clears.

questions.q: Dense fog covers the open (surface) portion of the line in the early morning. The standard operating precautions are:
options: Normal speeds, since cab signalling does everything
Restricted speed on the surface portion, greater spacing between trains, and extra care at level crossings and work sites where people rely on sight
Cancelling all trains till noon
Asking drivers to use headlights only
questions.explain: Fog removes the human eye as a safety layer — for staff on track, at crossings and at the lineside. Speed comes down so that what can be seen can still be stopped for.

questions.q: A train driver reports a trespasser walking on the track in an open section. The Operations Control Centre (OCC) response is:
options: Note it for the evening report
Caution or stop trains approaching that location, inform the nearest station and security to remove the person, and resume normal speed only after the track is confirmed clear
Ask the next driver to slow down and shout a warning
Wait for the person to leave on his own
questions.explain: A person on the track is a life-safety emergency in slow motion. Trains are protected at once, security removes the trespasser, and only a confirmed-clear report restores normal running.

questions.q: A hazardous chemical leak is reported from a factory next to a station, with fumes drifting towards it. The station's protective actions are:
options: Keep the station open so people can escape through it
Close station entries, have trains skip the station, shut or reconfigure ventilation so outside air is not drawn in, and follow the fire and police direction
Send staff outside to identify the chemical by smell
Evacuate passengers towards the factory side where buses wait
questions.explain: For an external gas threat the station becomes a sealed shelter problem: keep fumes out, keep people in safe air or move them on the clean side, and let the specialist agencies lead.
